title: Get back a commit you thought you lost

scenario.brief:
**What just happened.** You were cleaning up and ran `git reset --hard` one time too many. Your last commit — *"feat: finish invoice PDF"* — has vanished from the branch. The files are gone from your folder too. It feels like your afternoon's work is gone.

**It isn't.** Git almost never truly deletes a commit. For a while it keeps every commit your branch ever pointed at in a private diary called the **reflog** ("reference log"). Your lost commit is still in there.

**Your steps.**

1. Look at the diary: `git reflog`. Each line is a place HEAD used to be. You'll see your lost commit near the top, just before the reset.
2. Move your branch back to it: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (that means "where HEAD was one step ago"). Your commit — and its files — come right back.

Take a breath. This is recoverable.
scenario.whyItMatters: The scariest Git moment for beginners is thinking they destroyed work. Knowing the reflog turns panic into a thirty-second fix. Nothing you have committed is truly gone until Git's cleanup runs weeks later.

steps.message: feat: lay out the pdf header

objectives.title: Move your branch back to the lost commit
objectives.description: HEAD should point at "feat: finish invoice PDF" again.
hints: First see where HEAD has been: `git reflog`. The lost commit is the line just before the reset.
`HEAD@{1}` means 'where HEAD pointed one move ago' — that's your lost commit.

objectives.title: Your finished work is back in the folder
objectives.description: src/pdf.js should contain the render function again, with a clean working tree.
hints: A hard reset to the recovered commit brings its files back into your folder too.
Check with `git status` (clean) and open `src/pdf.js` — the render function should be there.
If files are still missing, you recovered the wrong point; try `git reset --hard` to the lost commit's id from `git reflog`.

debrief.summary: You recovered a commit that a hard reset had dropped, using the reflog — Git's record of everywhere your branch has been.
internals: `git reset --hard HEAD~1` moved your branch pointer back one commit and made your folder match it. The old commit wasn't deleted — nothing pointed at it any more, so it looked gone.
Git records every move of HEAD in `.git/logs/HEAD` — the reflog. Your lost commit's id was still sitting there.
`HEAD@{1}` asked the reflog for the commit HEAD pointed at one move ago. `reset --hard` to it moved your branch back and restored the files.
Unreferenced commits are only removed much later by `git gc`, so you have a long window to recover.

keyCommands.note: Everywhere HEAD has been, newest first. The lifeline after a bad reset.
Move the branch back to where HEAD was one step ago.
Move the branch to any commit id, e.g. one you found in the reflog.

commonMistakes: Assuming a hard reset deletes commits forever and giving up.
Reaching for the reflog too late is fine — but re-cloning or deleting the repo really does lose it.
Confusing HEAD@{1} (reflog position) with HEAD~1 (first parent).
debrief.atWork: Every engineer eventually resets, rebases or deletes a branch by mistake. The reflog is the first thing a calm teammate reaches for, and it has saved countless afternoons.
debrief.interview: "You ran git reset --hard and lost a commit. Now what?" Answer: git reflog to find it, then reset --hard (or branch) to that id.
